blocks.text: Ezra 9 opens with leaders bringing to Ezra a grave report: the people of Israel, priests, and Levites have not separated themselves from the surrounding peoples. Officials specify that both common people and nobles—taking daughters from Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites—have mingled the 'holy seed' with the peoples of the lands. Notably, the princes and rulers themselves stand foremost in this transgression.

Ezra's response is immediate and profoundly emotional. He tears his garment and robe, plucks out the hair of his head and beard, and sits down in shock and dismay. This physical expression of grief signals his perception of the situation as a crisis of grave spiritual consequence.

Ezra's visible distress summons an assembly: everyone who trembles at the words of the God of Israel gathers to him, stirred by the transgression of those returned from captivity. Ezra sits in confounded silence until the evening oblation, at which point he rises to offer prayer, still in his torn garments.

In his prayer, Ezra offers a corporate confession. He takes responsibility for the accumulated guilt of the people from their fathers' days forward, acknowledges that this iniquity caused their past subjection to foreign kings and captivity, yet expresses gratitude that God has not abandoned them in their bondage. He notes God's lovingkindness displayed through Persian favor, which has enabled the revival of their people and the restoration of God's house.
